headline: Computational rules for inferring viral host, structure and diversity face scrutiny
label: Viral Genomics Inference Methods
summary: Viral genomics increasingly relies on learned embeddings, structural alphabets, and pangenome graphs, making assignment-rule validity a practical concern.
synthesis: The common thread is scrutiny of the rules used to infer viral structure, host, lineage, and genome architecture from sequence and structural data. An H5Nx study finds that genotypes assigned by genetic similarity are incongruent with global phylogenies, directly questioning an assignment rule. VHAMSTeR predicts viral hosts across five kingdoms using fine-tuned genomic language model embeddings and reports outperforming prior methods. A structural informatics preprint uses structural-alphabet searches and structure similarity networks to map diverse GT-A glycosyltransferases across double-stranded DNA viruses, including a candidate jumbo-phage sulfated machinery. A comparative analysis reports a shared topological organisation among divergent intergenic RNAs, inferring function from structure rather than sequence conservation alone. PANIMaSTA builds minimally fragmented metagenomic pangenome variation graphs. What is new is explicit attention to whether inference steps are valid, not only whether model outputs score well. The items are heterogeneous, so this describes the dominant emphasis rather than a shared method.
